node.label: Angela Y. Davis
node.date_label: “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971) · Women, Race and Class (1981) · Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003)
node.description: A philosopher and activist whose writing ties the history of slavery to the politics of gender, class and punishment. In “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971), written in prison, she called the image of the Black matriarch “an open weapon of ideological warfare” and placed enslaved women at the centre of resistance to slavery. Women, Race and Class (1981) traces racism and class bias in the US women’s movement from abolition onward, and treats rape, reproductive freedom and housework through the inequalities between Black and white women. Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003) argues for decarceration and prison abolition. Johnnetta Cole’s 1972 response read the essay as a refutation of the matriarchy thesis’s “falsely assumed basis in slavery”, while noting that prison confined Davis to secondary sources. Saidiya Hartman (2016) describes feminist work on gender and reproduction in slavery as following the path the essay cleared, and Jennifer L. Morgan’s Reckoning with Slavery (2021) returns to it. Ruth Thrush (2025) recounts how Women, Race and Class criticised Silvia Federici’s case for wages for housework as reformist. Discussing her memoir Backtalker (2026), Kimberlé Crenshaw named Davis as an influence on her writing in the Black memoir tradition. Davis studied with Theodor Adorno in Frankfurt and says she was drawn to philosophy through Herbert Marcuse and the critical theory of the Frankfurt School.
node.representative_figures_and_works: If They Come in the Morning: Voices of Resistance (1971, with other political prisoners); “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971); Angela Davis: An Autobiography (1974); Women, Race and Class (1981); Blues Legacies and Black Feminism (1998); “Masked Racism: Reflections on the Prison Industrial Complex” (1998); Are Prisons Obsolete? (2003); Abolition Democracy: Beyond Empire, Prisons, and Torture (2005, interviews with Eduardo Mendieta); “Policing the Crisis Today” (2018).
node.scope_note: Only the last page of the 1971 essay was read (in the 1972 Massachusetts Review reprint). Women, Race and Class, Are Prisons Obsolete? and the 2018 chapter on Hall are represented by publisher descriptions and by named readers (Cole, Hartman, Morgan, Thrush, Crenshaw), not read directly. Her account of Frankfurt and critical theory rests on two published interviews. Her doctoral work with Marcuse is not documented on a permitted text read here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Reckoning with Slavery (2021), Morgan grounds her question about how enslaved women understood their own commodification in Davis’s “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971), which she calls important work.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Duke sample, introduction (“Refusing Demography”), p. 6, paragraph beginning “How does the concept of value”: “As early as 1971, the scholar and activist Angela Davis asked historians to consider the trauma that enslaved women experienced when they ‘had to surrender child-bearing to alien and predatory economic interests’” (n. 14); later in the paragraph, “To return to Davis’s important work, enslaved women were positioned to ‘attain a practical awareness’” of the slave owner’s power and dependence (n. 16). Body-text engagement in Morgan’s own framing of the book. The Morgan packet placed this on p. 7; the passage is on p. 6. Morgan’s chapters unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In a 2020 interview (published 2021), Davis recalls studying with Adorno in Frankfurt, loving his lectures and reading his works “voraciously”, while criticising his view that students should immerse themselves in theory rather than activism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Platypus Review 138, paragraphs beginning “That is basically how I got hooked on philosophy” (Marcuse “suggested that I study with Adorno, Horkheimer, and Habermas”), “I did learn a great deal about working within the context of contradictions” (“I loved his lectures, read his works voraciously”; “critical of him for his failure to recognize that it was possible at that moment”) and “Many of us felt that this stance did not reflect” (an “immanent critique of his stand with respect to activism”). A stated debt and a stated disagreement in Davis’s own spoken words. Formal supervision by Adorno is not stated here and is not claimed. Adorno’s texts unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Studied with Adorno; critical of his stance on activism

proposed_edges.relationship: Davis says she came to philosophy through the critical theory of Herbert Marcuse and the Frankfurt School, and that she has “certainly been inspired by critical theory” (interviews published 2005 and 2021).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Platypus Review 138 (interview of 7 December 2020), paragraph beginning “That is basically how I got hooked on philosophy”: she was drawn to “critical theory, which was the approach taken by Marcuse and the Frankfurt School of philosophy”, rather than analytical philosophy; paragraph beginning “This is one of the things I really appreciate about critical theory”. Abolition Democracy (2005) excerpt on the Seven Stories blog, answer beginning “Well, I’ve certainly been inspired by critical theory”, in which she credits Marcuse with crossing “the disciplinary borders that separate philosophy, sociology, and literature” and Adorno with bringing “music and philosophy into the conversation”. Stated debt in her own words. Her doctoral work and Marcuse’s supervision are not documented on a permitted text read here (Marcuse has no endpoint).

proposed_edges.relationship: Davis closes “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971) by quoting Du Bois’s Darkwater on Black women’s “revolutionary ideals”, and in Abolition Democracy (2005) says she has always preferred to identify with Du Bois’s pan-Africanism.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: (1) Massachusetts Review reprint, p. 100 (the essay’s last page): “Du Bois put it this way:” followed by a block quotation on “the up-working of new revolutionary ideals” among Black women, n. 46 “Du Bois, Darkwater, p. 185”. (2) Abolition Democracy excerpt (publisher’s blog), answer to “Do you think that there is a role for Black nationalism in the United States?”: “I’ve always preferred to identify with the pan-Africanism of W. E. B. Du Bois”, valued for its political, not racial, identification and its “Afro-Asian solidarities”. (3) Corroboration only: Crenshaw (2012), n. 1, says Davis’s account of the prison–industrial complex drew links to Du Bois’s assessment of Black imprisonment after Reconstruction (citing Women, Race & Class p. 89 on Black Reconstruction); that page is unread. Darkwater and Black Reconstruction not reread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Du Bois on Black women; Du Bois’s pan-Africanism

proposed_edges.relationship: In her contribution to Stuart Hall: Conversations, Projects and Legacies (2018), Davis argues, according to the publisher, that the model of politics, ideology and race developed by Hall and his Birmingham colleagues continues to resonate when applied to racialized policing in the United States.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Goldsmiths Press description, paragraph beginning “Throughout these pages, Hall’s colleagues and long-term collaborators”: “North American activist Angela Davis argues that the model of politics, ideology, and race initially developed by Hall and his colleagues in Birmingham continues to resonate when applied to America’s racialized policing.” Publisher description only; the chapter (listed among counted works as “Policing the Crisis Today”, 2018) is unread. The claim is limited to what the description states.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hall’s model applied to US policing

proposed_edges.relationship: Davis recalls seriously reading The Communist Manifesto at fifteen, in a class taught by a Marxist history teacher, and says that “embracing Marxism came rather naturally” (interview 2020, published 2021).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Platypus Review 138, paragraph beginning “My history teacher was a Marxist”: “At the age of 15, I seriously read The Communist Manifesto as a document we were studying in our class”; “Embracing Marxism came rather naturally.” She adds that it was not a moment of awakening but came “organically” from her upbringing and youth activism. A stated intellectual commitment in her own words, not a reading of specific Marxian arguments; the Manifesto is joint work with Engels. Thin; the coordinator may hold it if a self-described formation is judged too general.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Ruth Thrush’s account (2025), Davis’s Women, Race and Class (1981) is the most prominent critique of Federici’s wages-for-housework analysis: Thrush reads Davis as judging it reformist, because waged domestic workers already knew what wages for housework meant, and as proposing the socialization of housework instead.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Tribune, 20 October 2025, paragraph beginning “Since the publication of”: “Most prominently, Angela Davis, in her 1981 Women, Race and Class, argues that Federici’s analysis is markedly reformist”; Davis on domestic workers who “know better than anyone else what it means to receive wages for housework” and on a wage that would “further legitimize” women’s “domestic slavery”; paragraph beginning “In the place of wages” (socialization of housework). Thrush also argues the two are “closer than is often thought”. Mediated through Thrush’s account; Women, Race and Class is unread, and whether the chapter names Federici herself (or only the campaign) was not checked. Federici’s reply, if any, not found.

proposed_edges.relationship: Saidiya Hartman (2016) writes that feminist thinkers, following the path cleared by Davis’s “groundbreaking” 1971 essay on Black women in the community of slaves, have considered the significance of gender, sexuality and reproduction in the constitutive relations of slavery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hartman, “The Belly of the World”, authorised Vera List Center reprint, paragraph beginning “Black women’s labors have not been easy to reckon with conceptually”: “Feminist thinkers, following the path cleared by Angela Davis’ groundbreaking essay … have considered the significance of gender, sexuality and reproduction in defining the constitutive relations of slavery and the modes of its violence”, with n. 3 (Davis 1971 and two Hine articles). A named contribution in the body text of a substantive essay. Hartman does not discuss Davis’s argument further.

proposed_edges.relationship: Díaz Polegre and Torrado Martín-Palomino (2018) credit Davis with joining class to antiracist and antisexist perspectives in the 1970s, Women, Race and Class (1981) among the results, and name her among authors who had treated the concern before Crenshaw introduced the term intersectionality in 1989.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Investigaciones Feministas 9(2), p. 294, paragraph beginning “Angela Davis, figura emblemática”: “Durante la década de los años setenta Davis realizó aportaciones significativas a la perspectiva feminista al enlazar la clase social con la perspectiva antirracista y antisexista … siendo uno de los frutos de estas aportaciones su libro Mujeres, raza y clase (1981)” (attributed to Curiel 2009, p. 41); p. 297: the concern “había sido tratada por autoras como Angela Davis o Gloria Anzaldúa” (after Cruells 2015, p. 34). A substantive open-access article that names her contribution, but its claims are mediated through the authors it cites. Women, Race and Class unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Class, race and sex joined before the term

proposed_edges.relationship: Johnnetta Cole’s 1972 response calls Davis’s “Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves” (1971) a refutation of the Black matriarchy thesis’s “falsely assumed basis in slavery” and credits it with documenting enslaved women’s resistance, though written in prison from secondary sources only.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cole, “Affirmation of Resistance”, journal’s own PDF, p. 101: “The prime significance of the article is that it strikes at the heart of the so-called Black matriarchy issue through a refutation of its falsely assumed basis in slavery” (the myth “perpetuated in its fullest form by the ‘Moynihan Report’”); “the conditions of her imprisonment forced her to draw on secondary sources exclusively”; p. 103 (“In the cell of a California prison”). Davis’s own closing page (p. 100) corroborates the matriarchy argument. A substantive published response. Cole has no endpoint, so the claim is carried as a field contribution.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Belly of the World: A Note on Black Women’s Labors (2016), Saidiya Hartman identifies Angela Davis’s Reflections on the Black Woman’s Role in the Community of Slaves (1971) as a groundbreaking starting point for feminist analysis of gender, sexuality and reproduction in slavery.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Hartman’s argument on the Vera List Center’s own publication page, which identifies its 2017 conference publication, the original 2016 Souls article and permission to reprint. The Davis paragraph expressly credits the essay before considering the difficulty of incorporating enslaved women’s reproductive and domestic labor into narratives of Black radicalism. Note 3 supplies the 1971 year. This is a specific intellectual engagement and credit, not a claim that Davis supervised Hartman. Hartman’s wording varies the essay title; the relationship uses the title supplied in the Davis input. The journal’s full-text endpoint returned 403; no text was obtained there.
proposed_edges.map_label: Hartman credits Davis’s analysis of enslaved women

proposed_edges.relationship: In the 2020 panel transcript Where Do We Go From Here, Robin D. G. Kelley credits Angela Davis’s Abolition Democracy (2005) with proposing a vision of abolition democracy for a Third Reconstruction, as he develops his account of that project.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the opening question and Kelley’s first answer on Boston Review’s own transcript page. Kelley names Abolition Democracy, associates Davis’s argument with Du Bois’s abolition democracy and credits it in explaining his Third Reconstruction framework. He also credits William Barber; this is not an exclusive-origin claim. The 2005 original publication date was checked on Seven Stories Press’s book page. The complete Davis book was not read for this proposal.
proposed_edges.map_label: Kelley credits Abolition Democracy for a Third Reconstruction
